records.finding: Added the local processing evidence to the current event. The authors found seven rib spatulates in IV-2 and separate skinning evidence on MSA carnivore bones. A linked garment industry remains inference. El Mnasra and Dar es-Soltan I provide comparable artefacts from separate sites, without a demonstrated line of transfer. The catalogue’s Denisova needle and Bizmoune ornaments provide no instance of using these particular tools or hides.

sources.locator: pp. 3–6, Figs. 2–5, Tables S1–S3 and Discussion
sources.note: Primary study of spatulate wear, cut-mark distribution and the Moroccan comparative assemblages. Distinct physical proxies for processing, with clothing an inference.

sources.locator: Jacobs et al. 2011, abstract and Methods, pp. 3631–3643
sources.note: Original measurements of sediment dating. Jacobs is also a co-author of Hallett et al. This dates deposits and does not independently establish clothing.

records.next: Find a preserved piece, residue or independently examined use-wear that ties a particular tool to a garment or distinguishes the neighbouring spatulate traditions.

records.finding: Added the 2016 excavation report for the complete Main Chamber horizon 11.2 needle and microscopy of wear. The exact age, sewing material and human lineage remain open. The older East Chamber date belongs to a different bone. The 2025 excavation-author account reproduces the same object. At Canyars and the Great Basin there are other kinds of hide-work evidence, but no documented transfer from the Altai.

sources.note: Original excavation and traces, including the different contexts of the Main and East Chambers.

sources.locator: d’Errico et al. 2023, Abstract and Results
sources.note: Experimental and archaeological assessment of hide perforation at independent Canyars site, with no evidence that the Denisova needle supplied the technique.

sources.locator: Rosencrance et al. 2026, Results: Sewn hide and bone needles
sources.note: Independent US finds of sewn hide and needles, without evidence of direct descent from the Altai.

records.next: Match the needle’s horizon and sediment chronology, and look for preserved material or diagnostic use traces that identify a thread or product rather than inferring it from form alone.

records.finding: Replaced the source summary with the journal paper and updated the contextual date to the revised Period I envelope of c. 5250–4650 cal BCE. Grave 158 and the bead have no secure match to a direct date. The same site’s lost-wax amulet used a different method at a later date. Tel Tsaf and Dhuweila do not identify Mehrgarh as their cotton source. The Shahi Tump and Mohenjo-daro finds document other objects, with no demonstrated transfer from this burial community.

sources.locator: Moulherat et al. 2002, pp. 1393–1396, Figs. 2–4 and 7–9; pp. 1398–1400
sources.note: Primary fibre analysis. Identifies Period I grave MR.84.03.158 and gives the then-current chronology. The metal bead preserved the threads. This is not evidence for the origin of cotton plants or spinning devices.

sources.locator: Mutin et al. 2025, pp. 3–4, Fig. 2, and Discussion
sources.note: Independent lab measurements on teeth plus Bayesian modelling revise the site’s Period I sequence. Grave 158 was not identified in the inspected model. These are phase dates.

sources.locator: Liu et al. 2022, Results and discussion of cotton provenance
sources.note: Independent fibres from the Tel Tsaf site. The authors hypothesize a South Asian source from circumstantial evidence. They do not identify a Mehrgarh workshop, transmission route or specific producing community.

sources.locator: Betts et al. 1994, abstract
sources.note: Primary report of fabric impressions and fibres on lime plaster at Dhuweila. The tentative Levantine provenance comparison does not establish a particular source for this cloth.

records.next: Cross-reference burial 158 to the stratigraphic register and phase samples. Look for geographically diagnostic species or provenance evidence before linking Mehrgarh to the cotton finds farther west.

records.finding: Added the original museum laboratory report for silk in the W12 crossed-warp specimen, retained the press-reported approximate context date, and narrowed the record to woven material in the burial. The previous first-known and sericulture assignments were unsupported. Jiahu’s older soil proteins and possible textile tools cannot identify the source of Wanggou cloth or establish silkworm rearing. No evidence ties later Qianshanyang cloth to this settlement.

sources.note: Primary lab note separates a coarser plain weave and the finer, crossed-warp, ELISA-positive silk specimen in W12. No direct date here.

sources.locator: Zhou Yang interview, chronology of Wanggou sampling
sources.note: Investigator account distinguishes 2017 report from 2019 work. Substantially the same investigators as the museum lab source.

sources.locator: Age paragraph and sericulture discussion

records.next: Locate the W12 excavation stratigraphy and assay report with individual sample references, plus dated local textile tools, cocoon evidence or production traces that can establish how the silk was made.

records.finding: Added the topological identification of the Antrea knot from published drawings. Kaaronen et al. compare sheet bends at several northern European sites and explicitly leave convergence and transmission unresolved. The Järvensuo material is more than three millennia later. Neither the existing Maras cord nor Dzudzuana fibres document Antrea's manufacture or historical source. Kept the existing approximate date pending reconciliation of the net-bast and associated bark dates.

sources.locator: Kaaronen et al. 2025, pp. 479–481 and Fig. 1E
sources.note: Independent comparative reconstruction of Pälsi’s published knot. Its Antrea date derives from Manninen et al. 2021.

sources.note: New micro-CT observations on Järvensuo knots, different objects from Antrea. Its Antrea dating and willow-bast identification cite Miettinen et al. 2008.

sources.note: The primary Antrea dating and material report could not be opened through this route. Page locations are reported by Suomela et al.

records.next: Retrieve the original laboratory ages for the bast and floats with their material and context IDs. Compare orientation and mesh topology across dated nets to assess possible transmission against recurrent knotting.

records.finding: Retained the three-ply cord interpretation and contextual age. The fragment adhered to a flake. The connection between the artefacts during use is unresolved, so no link to local tool use or to the separate Dhaba Levallois record is proposed. The 2013 study reports earlier observations of different, fragmentary fibres by overlapping investigators. It cannot establish what the 2020 specimen did, or a line to the Antrea net.

sources.note: Primary fragment and microscopy, with contextual dating and interpretive limits.

sources.locator: Hardy et al. 2013, residue analysis and discussion of fibres
sources.note: Earlier observations on different samples at the same site, with overlapping authors. The complete cord fragment in the 2020 study is distinct.

records.next: Find an independently assessed similar fragment with a secure production or use association at the site or an attributable later context.

records.finding: Upgraded the original article, used its rounded 3800–3700 BCE wood date, and classified the Alpine evidence as a dated find. The report distinguishes surviving attachments, wear and reconstructed strands. The two laboratories tested wood from the same object. Neither later Alpine nor modern hide-webbed frames establish descent. Other Alpine wood rings in the paper have different sizes and ambiguous functions.

sources.note: Primary article text reproduced at source URL. Two reported determinations date the wood, while form, wear and context support the interpretation.

sources.note: Same article lineage as the hosted full text. The publisher's PDF download was unavailable in this pass.

records.next: Inspect the labs’ full calibration distributions and compare other securely dated frames and binding traces before proposing a lineage.

records.finding: Retained the Unit D interpretation and the species and function caveats. The 2011 site report distinguishes Unit D tools from the younger Unit C's richer evidence, and reuses the same team's fibre study. Awls and points in Unit D establish co-occurrence with the deposits, without an association to a particular fibre. Likeness to the Maras cord or later flax cloth does not identify a dependency.

sources.note: Original article hosted by the University of Georgia. Context gives the age; intended materials and fibre functions remain uncertain.
